documents: Published paper: Noël et al. (2022), Geophysical Research Letters 49, e2021GL095697 (PDF, 11 pages; Supporting Information not supplied)
pages_convention: PDF pages counted from 1 (identical to the printed 'n of 11' pagination)

entry.evidence: little is known about whether this slowdown is temporary, if it will persist or further strengthen in the future

steps.action: The authors take the post-2011 slowdown of Icelandic glacier mass loss from published in situ and satellite studies.
steps.quote: In sharp contrast, mass loss has slowed down since 2011

steps.action: They pose the question of whether the slowdown is temporary, will persist, or will strengthen in the future.
steps.quote: little is known about whether this slowdown is temporary, if it will persist or further strengthen in the future

steps.action: They reconstruct daily SMB for 1958-2019 with RACMO2.3 forced by ERA reanalyses and downscale it statistically to 500 m, using elevation gradients and MODIS albedo (method from the authors' earlier work).
steps.quote: that reconstructs the recent (1958–2019) and projects the future (1958–2099) SMB of Icelandic glaciers at 500 m spatial resolution

steps.action: They check the modelled 2 m air temperature against 51,833 daily measurements from 27 on-glacier automatic weather stations (R2 = 0.84, bias -0.48°C).
steps.quote: highlighting the ability of RACMO2.3 to represent the near-surface temperature above Icelandic glaciers

steps.action: They derive CryoSat-2 elevation and mass change (2011-2019) with a swath retrieval, basin hypsometry and assumed densities, and use the GRACE(-FO) mass series (2002-2019).
steps.quote: A swath retrieval algorithm similar to Garcia-Mondéjar et al. (2019) is used to estimate surface elevation from CryoSat-2 SARIn data (Baseline D)

steps.action: They estimate the annual SMB uncertainty (2.5 Gt/yr) by integrating fractional uncertainties over the accumulation and ablation areas.
steps.quote: The model annual SMB uncertainty (σ) is estimated at 2.5 Gt yr−1 on average for the period 1958–2019.

steps.action: They evaluate the SMB product against 1,196 stake records, ice-cap-integrated in situ mass change, GRACE and CryoSat-2, report the biases, and attribute part of them to the 11 km resolution and to non-surface processes.
steps.quote: The present-day SMB product has been thoroughly evaluated using a combination of in situ and remote sensing measurements

steps.action: They compare the reconstructed phases (balance until the mid-1990s, loss 1995-2010, slowdown from 2011) with previous in situ and satellite studies.
steps.quote: A shift to negative mass balance arises after 1995, in close agreement with independent in situ measurements

steps.action: They quantify the SMB components for 1958-1994, 1995-2010 and 2011-2019 and show that the changes in runoff drive the onset of mass loss and the later slowdown.
steps.quote: resulting in the post-2011 slowdown that essentially halved the mass loss relative to 1995–2010

steps.action: They regress SMB on runoff (R = 0.94) and runoff on glacier 2 m air temperature (R = 0.92) across years, using 5-yr running means.
steps.quote: variations in the SMB of Icelandic glaciers are mainly driven by fluctuations in meltwater runoff

steps.action: They correlate glacier 2 m air temperature with North Atlantic SST from ERA (R = 0.88 for 1958-2010), focusing on the Blue Blob region.
steps.quote: modelled Icelandic glacier 2 m air temperature strongly correlates with sea surface temperature (SST) measured by ERA reanalyses in the North Atlantic Ocean

steps.action: They map the 2011-2019 SST trend in ERA and define the Northern Blue Blob as the area of negative trend, which shows local cooling of up to -0.15°C/yr.
steps.quote: outlines the area as assumed to represent the Northern Blue Blob (NBB) in the North Atlantic Ocean

steps.action: They conclude that post-2011 cooling in the Northern Blue Blob reduced warming over the glaciers and so caused the slowdown of mass loss.
steps.quote: We conclude that the post-2011 development of the Blue Blob resulted in the slowdown of glacier mass loss in Iceland

steps.action: They run RACMO2.3 forced by CESM2 under SSP5-8.5 (1958-2099), downscaled to 500 m, to project SMB.
steps.quote: we use downscaled output of RACMO2.3-CESM2 under a high-end warming scenario

steps.action: They check that RACMO2.3-CESM2 reproduces the three historical SMB phases and the SST-temperature correlation patterns of RACMO2.3-ERA (difference ~4 Gt, same trend).
steps.quote: First we ascertained that RACMO2.3-CESM2 reproduces (1) Icelandic glaciers to be in approximate mass balance before 1995

steps.action: They report the projected Northern Blue Blob cooling of ~3°C until 2052, a ~2°C decrease in glacier air temperature, and a return of warming after the mid-2050s.
steps.quote: Under the SSP5-8.5 scenario, RACMO2.3-CESM2 projects sustained cooling in the NBB area from 2011 to 2052

steps.action: They interpret the asymmetric z-shaped correlation as a background warming plus a regional cooling perturbation; a linear fit gives Iceland ~60% of the Northern Blue Blob cooling, attributed to dissipation by air-mass advection.
steps.quote: We interpret the asymmetric cooling between ocean and atmospheric temperature as the superposition of a background warming trend with a superimposed regional perturbation

steps.action: They link the regional cooling to the published Warming Hole and AMOC-weakening and NAO explanations, noting that these remain uncertain.
steps.quote: has been linked to the development of the Warming Hole

steps.action: They compare their projection with Gervais et al. (2018), who also find Northern Blue Blob cooling until the 2050s and warming afterwards.
steps.quote: In line with our results, Gervais et al. (2018) projected a persistent cooling in the NBB until the 2050s

steps.action: They propose, without testing, that reduced transport of cold water and sea ice from the Labrador Sea and Fram Strait drives the post-2050s warming.
steps.quote: reduced cold water and sea ice transport from the Labrador Sea and Fram Strait into the NBB area

steps.action: They keep a three-stage projection: slowdown until the mid-2050s preserving ~200 Gt relative to the 1995-2010 trend, then -14.0 Gt/yr and ~30% volume loss by 2100.
steps.quote: Icelandic glaciers could preserve ∼200 Gt of ice (or 5% of the total volume) by the mid-2050s

tree.answer: Post-2011 slowdown of Icelandic glacier mass loss, known from prior observations
Partly: SMB is reconstructed by a model forced by reanalysis and evaluated against stakes and satellites
Identify the driver of the slowdown and project whether it persists in the 21st century
No rival drivers are stated or tested
No distinct predictions are derived for rivals
Conditions found: the historical climate (1958-2019) and one scenario run

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Interannual variability repeats; the correlations are fitted across years and stages
The product survives comparison with independent in situ and satellite data; no sensitivity to model, member or scenario is tested
Kept: Blue Blob cooling slows mass loss; mitigation projected until the mid-2050s

end.claim: Post-2011 cooling in the Northern Blue Blob of the North Atlantic is tied by a strong SST-air temperature-runoff-SMB relation to reduced Icelandic glacier mass loss, and under SSP5-8.5 it is projected to mitigate mass loss until the mid-2050s.

decisive_move.sentence: Without correlating glacier 2 m air temperature with Northern Blue Blob SST (R = 0.88), and through it with runoff and SMB, there would be no link between North Atlantic cooling and the slowdown.

gates.evidence: The model runs and data compilation serve the open persistence question, not a stated hypothesis. The SMB product faced independent stake, GRACE and CryoSat-2 tests it could have failed (p. 5-6), but the Blue Blob attribution was never tested against rival drivers (p. 7). The Northern Blue Blob region was defined from the same 2011-2019 ERA SST trend it is used to explain (Figure 3 caption, p. 7). Nothing is reported as fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Linear regression and correlation coefficients on 5-yr running means to link SMB, runoff, air temperature and SST

novelty_claims.quote: We use this new, daily data set, thoroughly evaluated using a combination of in situ
our new present-day SMB product accurately captures both the long-term mass loss trend and the seasonal cycle

limits: Sub-claims at other statuses: the 1958-2019 SMB reconstruction is estimate_with_resolution (uncertainty 2.5 Gt/yr, p. 5); the 21st-century three-stage projection is a single-scenario, single-GCM model projection with no status in the list (not forecast_skill, since it is not scored); the post-2050s mechanism (p. 9) is an untested hypothesis. The paper reports no sensitivity tests: one GCM (CESM2), apparently one ensemble member, one scenario (SSP5-8.5), and fixed downscaling and albedo choices. No rival drivers of the slowdown (precipitation, albedo or tephra, NAO-driven circulation alone) are tested; the causal attribution rests on correlation (inference). The NBB region is defined post hoc from the 2011-2019 negative SST trend, and correlations computed on 5-yr running means are likely inflated (inference). The Supporting Information (Figures S1-S5, Tables S1-S2) was not supplied, so steps that rely on it are coded from main-text descriptions. No review file was supplied, so no review sequence was coded. The paper does not say how the stage boundaries (2011, 2052/2053) were chosen.

disagreements.target: Gervais et al. (2018), CESM-LE projections of the North Atlantic warming hole
disagreements.support: The authors agree with the projected cooling-then-warming pattern but note that Gervais et al. do not identify the driver of the later warming, and they offer an untested hypothesis for it.
disagreements.quote: However, they do not identify the driving processes of the latter warming.
